name: Uma Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We're a mixed farm, two hundred and sixty acres. Forty suckler cows, a hundred ewes, potatoes, some barley, and the farm shop by the road that I run. Ray, my husband, does the fields and the stock, and I'm up at six doing the shop orders, then out to help him feed, then the shop opens at nine and I'm behind the counter till four, cutting cheese and hearing everybody's news.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The shop is the best part. Mrs Patel comes every Thursday for six eggs and twenty minutes of talk, and I wouldn't miss it. What wears me out is that it never stops. Saturdays in December we do the turkey orders and I'm on my feet twelve hours, and I'm not thirty any more.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two women in the shop part-time, Jean and Kirsty, both from the village. Our daughter Nadia runs a hair salon in town and our son Tim is a train driver. Neither wants the farm, which is fine, we've sort of made our peace with that.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any computers or AI in the business?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The till, the card machine, which took me three years to agree to, and Kirsty does our page on the internet. I've never used AI and I don't intend to. If I want to know something I ring someone who knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, nothing changes, now can we get back to work. I'd say it to the customers too, they love talking about the news over the counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing. If prices and wages carry on as normal, the shop carries on as normal. People still want proper sausages and someone to ask how their hip is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as every year. Repaint the shop sign, which is long overdue. Put the price of lamb up by the usual ten pence a kilo in spring. Maybe let Kirsty try her AI thing on the shop's page, if she must.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit smug, actually, because I've been saying this would all blow over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your life is most excited about this AI business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kirsty, without a doubt. She's twenty-eight and she's always showing me things on her phone. Last week it wrote a poem about our sausages. I told her the sausages don't need poems, they need people to buy them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever let her use it for the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the page on the internet, yes, as long as I read it first. Not for anything with my name on a letter. My customers know how I write, and they'd know if it wasn't me.

S0.say: I'd say good, nothing changes, now let's get back to work. I'd say it to customers over the counter too, because they love chatting about the news.
S0.think: It means nothing to me. If prices and wages carry on, the shop carries on, because people still want proper sausages and someone to ask how their hip is.
S0.do: Repaints the long-overdue shop sign and raises the lamb price by the usual ten pence a kilo in spring. Lets her shop worker Kirsty try AI on the shop's web page, as long as she reads it first.
S0.feel: Calm and a little smug, since she always said the fuss would blow over.
S0.quote: Last week it wrote a poem about our sausages. I told her the sausages don't need poems, they need people to buy them.
S0.fieldNote: Uma is brisk and warm, and the shop counter is her stage. She sees the business as relationships, not transactions. She allows the technology at arm's length, under her own eye.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's sense on both sides. Some things will get easier and some young people will struggle to get a start. The government should do something sensible in the middle, if they can manage that, which I doubt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slow is fine by me. I'm fifty-eight, it'll barely reach the farm before I'm done. What bothers me is Kirsty, really. She's bright, and she keeps applying for office jobs in town. If those beginner jobs dry up, she'll stay in my shop forever, which is nice for me and bad for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new on the farm. I'd keep the shop exactly as it is. I'd maybe give Kirsty a bit more responsibility, put her in charge of the online orders officially, with a rise of a pound an hour, so she's got something to put on her CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy for the young ones. For me, nothing much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kirsty if she got turned down again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cup of tea in the back, and I'd tell her she's worth more than they think. Then I'd tell her to go and see the man at the agricultural college, because they're always short of people who understand both farms and computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government should do something sensible. What would sensible look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paying firms a bit to take on young people, like they did years ago. My Tim got his first job that way at the railway. I'm not for big promises, just something that works and doesn't cost the earth.

S1.say: There's sense on both sides: some things get easier, and some young people struggle to get a start. The government should do something sensible in the middle, if it can.
S1.think: Slow is fine for me, because it'll barely reach the farm before I'm done. What bothers me is Kirsty, who keeps applying for office jobs and could end up stuck in my shop.
S1.do: Keeps the farm and shop exactly as they are. Puts Kirsty officially in charge of online orders with a rise of a pound an hour, so she has something for her CV, and points her to the agricultural college.
S1.feel: A little uneasy for young people, and not worried for herself.
S1.quote: If those beginner jobs dry up, she'll stay in my shop forever, which is nice for me and bad for her.
S1.fieldNote: Her centre politics show as a wish for something sensible that works, based on her own son's experience of a job scheme. She is honest that keeping Kirsty suits her. Her care for staff is personal, not political.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the politicians should stop shouting and sit down and sort it out. People losing office jobs need help, but I don't trust anyone who says there's an easy answer, left or right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd worry for the shop. Half my customers work in offices in town, at the council and the building society. If they're laid off or their pay is squeezed, the first thing to go is the twelve-pound joint of beef from the farm shop. They'll buy it at the supermarket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watch the takings every week, closer than I do now. If they dropped by a fifth, I'd cut the shop to five days and keep Jean and Kirsty on fewer hours rather than let one go. Bring in a cheaper sausage line, plain pork, to keep people coming through the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not about robots or computers, about the shop going quiet. A quiet shop is the worst feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a quiet shop feel like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I had one in the bad winter of 2009. I'd stand there and listen to the fridge humming and count the cars going past without stopping. I lost half a stone that winter from worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got savings behind you. Does that help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, we'd be all right. We could close the shop tomorrow and not starve. But the shop isn't about money, not really. It's the reason anyone comes up our lane.

S2.say: The politicians should stop shouting and sort it out. People losing office jobs need help, but I don't trust anyone who says there's an easy answer, left or right.
S2.think: I'd worry for the shop, because half my customers work in offices in town. If their pay is squeezed, the first thing to go is the twelve-pound joint of beef from my counter.
S2.do: Checks the shop takings weekly and, if they fall by a fifth, cuts to five days while keeping both staff on fewer hours. Adds a cheaper plain pork sausage line to keep people coming in.
S2.feel: Anxious about the shop going quiet, not about computers.
S2.quote: I'd stand there and listen to the fridge humming and count the cars going past without stopping.
S2.fieldNote: The threat she sees is entirely about her customers' wallets, which is very concrete. Her savings mean the worry isn't about money, it's about the shop as the farm's social heart. Her memory of 2009 gives the fear a real shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say both sides have a point. The people who made the AI should keep some of the gains, but not all of it. Something in between, like a fair tax, and stop the shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the shop would split in two. The people with shares and big houses would buy more, the hamper at Christmas, the whole fillet. The ones who lost their jobs would stop coming. I'd see the whole crisis from behind my counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Change what the shop stocks. Put in a posher range for the well-off, and keep a cheap counter for everyone else, with a soup-and-bread deal at three pounds. Keep both staff. Not invest anything big, because a boom that fast makes me nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit sad. I don't like the idea of my customers being split into the haves and have-nots, standing next to each other in my queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when you see someone you know who's lost their job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put an extra few sausages in their bag and say nothing. I've done it before. Mr Hughes from the building society, when his wife was ill, he'd never have asked. You just do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said both sides have a point. Is there a side you'd lean to if you had to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If you pushed me, I'd say tax the people who got rich fastest a bit more. But I'd want it to go to things you can see, like the village bus and the surgery. Not into some fund nobody understands.

S3.say: Both sides have a point. The people who made the AI should keep some of the gains, but not all, so something in between like a fair tax, and stop the shouting.
S3.think: The shop would split in two, with the well-off buying hampers and fillet and the jobless stopping coming. I'd see the whole crisis from behind my counter.
S3.do: Splits the shop's range into a posher line and a cheap counter with a three-pound soup and bread deal. Keeps both staff and avoids any big investment, wary of a boom that fast.
S3.feel: Uneasy and a bit sad at seeing her customers split into haves and have-nots in the same queue.
S3.quote: I'd put an extra few sausages in their bag and say nothing.
S3.fieldNote: She experiences national politics through her shop queue, which gives her a very grounded view. Pushed, she leans towards taxing the fastest-rich, but only for visible local things. Her quiet kindness to customers in trouble is a pattern, not a one-off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say not everything should be done by a machine, and people will pay for real hands. I'd put a sign up: everything here grown and made by people. That'd be my answer, not shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it frightens me, because Ray's sixty and his knees are going, and the robots could do the lifting he can't. Part of me would want one. But if the big farms get robots and sell lamb at half the price, my shop is finished, and the shop is the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not buy a robot, not in the first year. Watch what happens. Put the sign up and make the most of being the farm where people still work. Sit down with Ray and the accountant and work out what the place is worth, in case we need to sell in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, mostly of the shop going. And a bit angry that something I can't vote on could undo forty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jean and Kirsty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're not getting robots, not while I'm behind that counter. Jean's sixty-two and she'd retire anyway. Kirsty I'd worry about, because her other choice would be the supermarket, and if the supermarket has robots too, where does she go?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said part of you would want one for Ray. Which part wins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. If he did his back in, I'd buy one the next week, I expect. That's the honest answer. I'd hate it, but I'd buy it.

S4.say: Not everything should be done by a machine, and people will pay for real hands. I'd put a sign up saying everything here is grown and made by people.
S4.think: It frightens me. Ray's knees are going and part of me would want a robot for the lifting, but if big farms sell lamb at half the price, my shop is finished, and the shop is the farm.
S4.do: Holds off buying a robot in the first year and markets the shop as the farm where people still work. Has the accountant value the farm with Ray in case they need to sell within a couple of years.
S4.feel: Scared of losing the shop, and angry that something she can't vote on could undo forty years.
S4.quote: If he did his back in, I'd buy one the next week, I expect. That's the honest answer. I'd hate it, but I'd buy it.
S4.fieldNote: Her resistance has a clear limit: her husband's health. She turns her fear into a selling point with the people-made sign, which fits her shop instincts. The thought of the shop closing reaches her more than any money worry.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one, because of the shop. What would help is honest labels, so customers know what was made by people and what wasn't, and some help for small farm shops, like lower business rates. Nothing fancy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the old people. Half my Thursday customers live on their own. The shop is the only conversation some of them have all week. No robot is going to ask Mrs Patel about her hip.

headlineQuote: No robot is going to ask Mrs Patel about her hip.
portrait: Uma Yilmaz is fifty-eight and runs the farm shop on a mixed family farm of cattle, sheep, potatoes and barley, while her husband Ray works the fields. She has never used AI, took three years to accept a card machine, and judges every change by what it does to her shop counter. Her politics are firmly in the middle, impatient with shouting from either side. In the office and fast pictures, she sees the crisis through her customers' spending and quietly slips extra sausages into bags. The robot picture frightens her because it threatens the shop, though she admits she'd buy one if Ray hurt his back.
biggestWorry: The robots picture, because cheap robot-farmed meat could close her farm shop, which is the heart of the farm.
whatWouldHelp: Honest labels showing what was made by people, and practical support for small farm shops such as lower business rates.
